claim: Many funding agencies and journals now mandate the inclusion of females as well as males in biomedical studies.
source: To enhance inclusivity and rigor, many funding agencies and journals now mandate the inclusion of females as well as males in biomedical studies.
evidence: This is stated as a current practice in the abstract without specific citations, but is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Study designs, analyses, and interpretations of results in sex-inclusive research are often flawed.
source: Education in sound methods to consider sex as a subgroup category has lagged behind, however, resulting in a problematic literature in which study designs, analyses, and interpretations of results are often flawed.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript (Patsopoulos et al., 2007; Zell et al., 2015; Wallach et al., 2016; Kaul, 2017; David et al., 2018; Eliot et al., 2021; Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021; Maney et al., 2023; Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023).

claim: The US government has mandated the inclusion of women in clinical investigations since 1993.
source: In response to an historical exclusion of women from biomedical studies and trials, the US government has mandated the inclusion of women in clinical investigations since 1993 (Epstein, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Epstein, 2007.

claim: Researchers funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the US have been required to include females and males in preclinical non-human animal studies since 2016.
source: Similarly, researchers funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the US have been required to include females and males in preclinical non-human animal studies since 2016 (Clayton and Collins, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clayton and Collins, 2014.

claim: Similar sex-inclusive policies have been implemented in Canada and Europe.
source: Similar sex-inclusive policies have been implemented in Canada and Europe, and many journals now require the inclusion of females and males unless otherwise justifiable (Health Canada, 2023; Heidari et al., 2016; NIH, 2015a; White et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Health Canada, 2023; Heidari et al., 2016; NIH, 2015a; White et al., 2021.

claim: On average, men and women differ in the incidence and presentation of disease, risk factors for disease, treatment response and adverse drug reactions.
source: The rationale for such policies is founded on observations that, on average, men and women differ in the incidence and presentation of disease, risk factors for disease, treatment response and adverse drug reactions, as well as on the belief that similar, undiscovered differences may be widespread (van Anders, 2022; Clayton, 2018; Karp et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Anders, 2022; Clayton, 2018; Karp et al., 2017.

claim: Differences between men and women have been reported in the incidence and average age of onset of auto-immune diseases such as lupus and multiple sclerosis.
source: Indeed, differences between men and women have been reported in the incidence and average age of onset of many diseases, notably auto-immune diseases such as lupus and multiple sclerosis (Voskuhl, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voskuhl, 2011.

claim: Differences between men and women have been reported in mental health conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.
source: mental health conditions such as depression (SAMHSA, 2012) and schizophrenia (Abel et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to SAMHSA, 2012 and Abel et al., 2010.

claim: Differences between men and women have been reported in substance use disorders.
source: substance use disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; Becker and Koob, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McHugh et al., 2018; Becker and Koob, 2016.

claim: Differences between men and women have been reported in cardiovascular disease.
source: and cardiovascular disease (Oneglia et al., 2020; Mosca et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oneglia et al., 2020; Mosca et al., 2011; Ji et al., 2022.

claim: Diabetes and cigarette smoking are more potent risk factors for cardiovascular disease among women.
source: Diabetes and cigarette smoking are more potent risk factors for cardiovascular disease among women (Humphries et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Humphries et al., 2017.

claim: Women are more likely to present with atypical symptoms of coronary heart disease than are men.
source: and women are more likely to present with atypical symptoms of coronary heart disease than are men (Canto et al., 2012; Mieres et al., 2011; Eastwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Canto et al., 2012; Mieres et al., 2011; Eastwood et al., 2013.

claim: In 2013, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommended lower dosing of the prescription drug zolpidem for women than for men, citing higher blood levels of the drug in women eight hours after it was taken.
source: In 2013, for example, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommended lower dosing of the prescription drug zolpidem for women than for men, citing higher blood levels of the drug in women eight hours after it was taken (FDA, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to FDA, 2018.

claim: Women are now represented in most clinical trials.
source: As a result of the policies to increase inclusion, women are now represented in most clinical trials (Bierer and Meloney, 2022; Sosinsky et al., 2022; Feldman et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bierer and Meloney, 2022; Sosinsky et al., 2022; Feldman et al., 2019.

claim: Preclinical research increasingly includes female animals.
source: and preclinical research increasingly includes female animals (Beery and Zucker, 2011; Woitowich et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beery and Zucker, 2011; Woitowich et al., 2020.

claim: The NIH policy on sex as a biological variable (SABV) explicitly states that although data must be disaggregated by sex, statistical comparisons are not required.
source: The NIH policy on sex as a biological variable (SABV), for example, explicitly states that although data must be disaggregated by sex, statistical comparisons are not required (NIH, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NIH, 2020.

claim: Most researchers who comply with SABV do compare the sexes.
source: Nonetheless, most researchers who comply with SABV do compare the sexes (Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021.

claim: The practice of comparing sexes appears to have led to a large increase in the number of differences reported.
source: and this practice appears to have led to a large increase in the number of differences reported (Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023.

claim: Many claims of sex differences are based on flawed study designs, analyses or interpretations of results.
source: Indeed, it is becoming more apparent that many claims of sex differences are based on flawed study designs, analyses or interpretations of results (Patsopoulos et al., 2007; Zell et al., 2015; Wallach et al., 2016; Kaul, 2017; David et al., 2018; Eliot et al., 2021; Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021; Maney et al., 2023; Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Patsopoulos et al., 2007; Zell et al., 2015; Wallach et al., 2016; Kaul, 2017; David et al., 2018; Eliot et al., 2021; Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021; Maney et al., 2023; Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023.

claim: Training in methods to detect sex differences has not kept pace with the unprecedented opportunity to investigate them.
source: The widespread use of suboptimal approaches suggests that training in methods to detect sex differences has not kept pace with the unprecedented opportunity to investigate them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of widespread suboptimal approaches.

claim: NIH distinguishes studies 'intended to test for sex differences' from those that are not.
source: In its guide to reviewers, NIH distinguishes studies "intended to test for sex differences" from those that are not, seemingly marshalling two different approaches (NIH, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NIH, 2015b.

claim: The NIH requires only studies intended to test for sex differences to have the statistical power and analytic methods adequate to the task.
source: The NIH requires only studies intended to test for sex differences to have the statistical power and analytic methods adequate to the task; others are not held to such expectations – that is, their approach to sex as a variable may be more exploratory in nature (NIH, 2015b; NIH, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to NIH, 2015b; NIH, 2020.

claim: Exploratory studies typically include neither a priori hypotheses nor sample sizes large enough to test for effects within or between subgroups.
source: In general, exploratory studies typically include neither a priori hypotheses nor sample sizes large enough to test for effects within or between subgroups (Schwab and Held, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schwab and Held, 2020.

claim: An underpowered, within-subgroup analysis does not meet basic standards of analytical rigor and threatens reproducibility.
source: As we explain below, an underpowered, within-subgroup analysis does not meet basic standards of analytical rigor, even when taking an exploratory approach to sex differences, and therefore threatens reproducibility (Rich Edwards et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rich Edwards et al., 2018.

claim: Studies not designed to interrogate sex differences are often poorly equipped to test alternative explanations for sex effects, such as confounding by gender.
source: Furthermore, studies not designed to interrogate sex differences are often poorly equipped to test alternative explanations for sex effects, such as confounding by gender (Ritz and Greaves, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ritz and Greaves, 2022.

claim: An explosion of exploratory analyses will maximize false positive discoveries.
source: Finally, while an explosion of exploratory analyses will undoubtedly promote discovery of sex differences, they will also maximize false positive discoveries (Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023.

claim: Gender encompasses identity, expression, and sociocultural expectations and affects human health.
source: Second, we note that gender – which encompasses identity, expression, and sociocultural expectations – also affects human health and is already the subject of directives in some countries (Health Canada, 2023; NASEM, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Health Canada, 2023; NASEM, 2022.

claim: Sex is not itself a tangible, single variable; it is simply a proxy for many factors that covary imperfectly with each other.
source: Sex is not itself a tangible, single variable; it is simply a proxy for many factors that covary imperfectly with each other (Richardson, 2022; Maney, 2016; Massa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Richardson, 2022; Maney, 2016; Massa et al., 2023.

claim: Sex and gender nearly always confound each other in human studies.
source: Sex and gender thus nearly always confound each other in human studies.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle based on the relationship between sex and gender.

claim: Non-human animals can experience sex-specific environmental factors such as housing density, aggression from conspecifics, and access to resources.
source: Even non-human animals, regardless of whether they experience something we could call gender, can experience sex-specific environmental factors such as housing density, aggression from conspecifics, access to resources, and so on Cortes et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cortes et al., 2019.

claim: Comparing the sexes by qualitatively comparing within-sex p-values fails to actually contrast the sexes.
source: Unfortunately, many studies fumble the three-variable question (sex/treatment/outcome) by turning it into a pair of two-variable problems (treatment/outcome for males and treatment/outcome for females); this practice of qualitatively comparing the within-sex p-values fails to actually contrast the sexes.
evidence: This is a methodological principle explained by the authors.

claim: The practice of qualitatively comparing within-sex p-values has been called one of the most common statistical mistakes in science.
source: In fact, we have not directly compared the treatment effect between the sexes at all. We have instead committed a logical error so widespread among subgroup analyses that it has been called out as one of the most common statistical mistakes in science (Makin and Orban de Xivry, 2019; Allison et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makin and Orban de Xivry, 2019; Allison et al., 2016.

claim: The difference in sex-specific significance (DISS) error is rampant in the context of sex differences.
source: In the context of sex differences, where it is rampant, we have proposed calling it the difference in sex-specific significance (DISS) error (Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023.

claim: In a study with 80% power to detect a treatment effect in the entire sample, there is typically only 50% power to detect a within-sex treatment effect.
source: Consider, for example, an experiment with equal numbers of males and females designed to have 80% statistical power to detect a non-null (P<0.05) treatment effect in the entire sample. Such a study typically has only 50% power to detect a within-sex treatment effect.
evidence: This is a statistical principle explained by the authors.

claim: When the treatment effect is non-null and does not vary by sex, the likelihood of one group yielding P<0.05 and the other P>0.05 is 50% in a study with 80% power overall and 50% power within sex.
source: Under this common scenario, when the treatment effect is non-null and does not, in fact, vary by sex, the likelihood of one group yielding P<0.05 and the other P>0.05 is 50% (Bland and Altman, 2011; George et al., 2016; Brookes et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bland and Altman, 2011; George et al., 2016; Brookes et al., 2004.

claim: The DISS approach is biased toward false positive findings.
source: But, although the DISS approach is biased toward false positive findings (Bland and Altman, 2011; George et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bland and Altman, 2011; George et al., 2016.

claim: The DISS approach can produce false negatives and cause investigators to miss real sex differences.
source: it can also produce false negatives – that is, it can cause investigators to miss real sex differences (left panel of Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B.

claim: In a study of abdominal obesity in children, authors missed a large sex difference in the association between AO and a measure of lipoprotein particle number because their within-sex p-values showed non-significant associations in both girls and boys.
source: For example, in a recent study of abdominal obesity in children (AO), the authors missed a large sex difference in the association between AO and a measure of lipoprotein particle number because their within-sex p-values showed non-significant associations in both girls and boys (Akiyama et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Akiyama et al., 2022.

claim: In the abdominal obesity study, the interaction between sex and AO was highly significant (P=0.001); the association in girls was positive and among boys, negative.
source: In fact, the interaction between sex and AO was highly significant (P=0.001); the association in girls was positive and among boys, negative (Vorland et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vorland et al., 2023.

claim: Including sex as a variable in the statistical model can have the added advantage of unmasking effects of treatment when the effect is much larger in one sex than another or goes in different directions in each sex.
source: Including sex in the statistical model can have the added advantage of unmasking effects of treatment when the effect is much larger in one sex than another or goes in different directions in each sex (Phillips et al., 2023; Buch et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2023; Buch et al., 2019.

claim: The main effect of sex is often confused with the sex-by-treatment interaction term.
source: We should point out here that the main effect of sex is often confused with the sex-by-treatment interaction term; that is, a significant main effect of sex is misinterpreted as a sex difference in the response to treatment (Eliot et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eliot et al., 2023.

claim: The mistaken interpretation of the outputs of analyses of variance (ANOVAs) is common.
source: This mistaken interpretation of the outputs of analyses of variance (ANOVAs) is common (Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Garcia-Sifuentes and Maney, 2021.

claim: The mistaken interpretation of ANOVA outputs has been endorsed in NIH training materials about how to incorporate sex as a variable into research designs.
source: and, notably, has been endorsed even in NIH training materials about how to incorporate sex as a variable into research designs (NIH, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NIH, 2020.

claim: Findings of sex differences are often used by non-scientists and scientists alike to shape public policy.
source: Findings of sex differences are often used by non-scientists and scientists alike to shape public policy (Maney, 2015; Maney, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maney, 2015; Maney, 2016.

claim: Statistical interactions can require notoriously large sample sizes to detect.
source: First, statistical interactions can require notoriously large sample sizes to detect (Galea et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galea et al., 2020.

claim: Kent and colleagues estimated that only one in four subgroup interactions observed in exploratory analyses are true positives.
source: Kent and colleagues estimated that only one in four subgroup interactions observed in exploratory analyses are true positives (Kent et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kent et al., 2018.

claim: At least one treatment has been made less available to women in the US on the basis of 'sex differences' that are relatively small and of controversial importance.
source: At this time, at least one treatment has been made less available to women in the US on the basis of "sex differences" that are relatively small and of controversial importance (Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2023.

claim: Availability of other treatments and preventatives are in danger of being similarly curtailed for women without sufficient evidence.
source: Availability of other treatments and preventatives are in danger of being similarly curtailed for women without sufficient evidence (Denly, 2021; Tadount et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Denly, 2021; Tadount et al., 2020.

claim: The recent dramatic increase in reports of sex differences is encouraging but concerning.
source: Thus, although the recent dramatic increase in reports of sex differences (Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023) is encouraging, it is at the same time concerning.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maney and Rich-Edwards, 2023.

claim: Many authors have called for new ways of operationalizing and conceptualizing sex, not as a way to deny or minimize sex differences but rather to increase precision in science.
source: Many authors have called for new ways of operationalizing and conceptualizing sex, not as a way to deny or minimize sex differences but rather to increase precision in our science (Ritz and Greaves, 2022; Richardson, 2022; Joel and Fausto-Sterling, 2016; Hyde et al., 2019; Massa et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ritz and Greaves, 2022; Richardson, 2022; Joel and Fausto-Sterling, 2016; Hyde et al., 2019; Massa et al., 2023.

claim: The effect of treatment is statistically significant for males (P=0.036) but not for females (P=0.342) in the dataset shown in Figure 2A left panel.
source: The effect of treatment is statistically significant for males (*P=0.036) but not for females (P=0.342)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The sex × treatment interaction is not statistically significant (P=0.496) in the dataset shown in Figure 2A.
source: The sex × treatment interaction is not statistically significant (P=0.496), meaning there is no evidence that males and females responded differently and no justification to test for effects of treatment separately within each sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The main effect of treatment is significant (P=0.034) in the dataset shown in Figure 2A, suggesting that the treatment altered the outcome measure irrespective of sex.
source: The main effect of treatment, which is estimated from all subjects combined, is significant (P=0.034) suggesting that the treatment altered the outcome measure irrespective of sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Figure 2B, the effect of treatment is not statistically significant within females (P=0.115) or within males (P=0.185).
source: The effect of treatment is not statistically significant within females (P=0.115) or within males (P=0.185)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Figure 2B, the sex × treatment interaction is statistically significant (P=0.038), indicating the difference in the responses of females and males.
source: The sex × treatment interaction, which is statistically significant (P=0.038), indicates the difference in the responses of females and males.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The recommendations are organized within the '4 Cs of Studying Sex to Strengthen Science: Consideration, Collection, Characterization and Communication,' a framework developed by the Office of Research on Women's Health at the National Institutes of Health in the United States.
source: Our recommendations are organized within the "4 Cs of Studying Sex to Strengthen Science: Consideration, Collection, Characterization and Communication," a framework developed by the Office of Research on Women's Health at the National Institutes of Health in the United States.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the framework's origin.

claim: The 4 Cs framework calls upon researchers to: Consider sex in study design; Collect sex-based data; Characterize sex-based data in analysis; and Communicate sex-based data through publication.
source: This framework calls upon researchers to: Consider sex in study design; Collect sex-based data; Characterize sex-based data in analysis; and Communicate sex-based data through publication.
evidence: This describes the components of the 4 Cs framework.

claim: The principles outlined in this article apply to observational studies as well as experiments and clinical trials, and apply equally to pre-clinical, clinical and population science.
source: First, the principles outlined here apply to observational studies as well as experiments and clinical trials, and apply equally to pre-clinical, clinical and population science.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle by the authors.

claim: The same research principles outlined in this article apply to the study of gender or any other subgroup.
source: While this article highlights sex as the focus of current federal mandates in the US, the same research principles outlined below apply to the study of gender or any other subgroup.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle by the authors.

claim: Ignoring an entire sex or gender in research design, data analysis, and reporting, without strong justification, is arguably incompatible with rigorous or generalizable science.
source: This change is a welcome and needed corrective; ignoring an entire sex or gender in research design, data analysis, and reporting, without strong justification, is arguably incompatible with rigorous or generalizable science.
evidence: This is stated as a principle by the authors.

claim: For many researchers, including females and males represents a novel approach for which training could be lacking.
source: For many researchers, including females and males represents a novel approach for which training could be lacking (Maney et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maney et al., 2023.

claim: The NIH effectively proposes two standards to which NIH-funded studies can be held by distinguishing exploratory studies from those designed to interrogate a sex difference.
source: In differentiating exploratory studies from those designed to interrogate a sex difference, the NIH effectively proposes two standards to which NIH-funded studies can be held.
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors of NIH policy.

claim: The distinction between exploratory and confirmatory research has a long history.
source: The distinction between exploratory and confirmatory research has a long history that is useful to consider in the context of recent mandates (Forstmeier et al., 2017; Wagenmakers et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Forstmeier et al., 2017; Wagenmakers et al., 2012.

claim: Authors of confirmatory studies are motivated by preliminary data or prior literature to specify clear testable hypotheses, prespecify subgroup contrasts, and size their studies to formally test for subgroup differences.
source: In contrast, authors of confirmatory studies are motivated by preliminary data or prior literature to specify clear testable hypotheses, prespecify subgroup contrasts, and size their studies to formally test for subgroup differences.
evidence: This describes characteristics of confirmatory studies.

claim: The trouble comes in the expectation that within-sex analyses should be conducted in all studies – even those not adequately powered or designed to examine how treatment effects vary by sex.
source: The trouble comes in the expectation that within-sex analyses should be conducted in all studies – even those not adequately powered or designed to examine how treatment effects vary by sex (NIH, 2020; CIHR, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to NIH, 2020; CIHR, 2023.

claim: It is better to measure sex-related variables, such as hormones or gene expression, than to reason backwards from sex to speculative biologic mechanisms when possible.
source: When possible, it is better to measure sex-related variables, such as hormones or gene expression, than to reason backwards from sex to speculative biologic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a recommendation by the authors.

claim: The effects of gender expression, gendered occupations, and disparities in access to health care can be challenging to disentangle from manifestations of 'sex.'
source: The effects of gender expression, gendered occupations, and disparities in access to health care can be challenging to disentangle from manifestations of 'sex,' not only because the construct of gender is complex but also because it is exquisitely sensitive to place and time (Nielsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2021.

claim: A significant main effect of sex simply means that there is a sex difference in the incidence of heart disease, not that there is a sex difference in the efficacy of aspirin.
source: In the example above regarding the effect of aspirin on heart disease, a significant sex-by-treatment interaction would provide evidence that the effect of aspirin on heart disease differed between men and women; in contrast, a significant main effect of sex simply means that there is a sex difference in the incidence of heart disease. It does not indicate a sex difference in the efficacy of aspirin.
evidence: This is an explanation of statistical concepts by the authors.

claim: Not all sex differences, even statistically significant ones, are large enough to be important.
source: We caution that not all sex differences, even statistically significant ones, are large enough to be important.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors.

claim: Big data analyses often have enough statistical power to unearth truly trivial sex differences.
source: Big data analyses in particular often have enough statistical power to unearth truly trivial sex differences.
evidence: This is an observation by the authors about big data analyses.

claim: Whether a sex difference is clinically meaningful or actionable depends very much on context and must be judged on the size of the difference, not the size of the p-value.
source: Whether a sex difference is clinically meaningful or actionable depends very much on context and must be judged on the size of the difference, not the size of the p-value (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known) is a posteriori justification of an unplanned result that is hard for readers to detect unless study protocols are pre-registered.
source: We must avoid the temptation of HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known; Kerr, 1998); such a posteriori justification of an unplanned result is hard for readers to detect unless study protocols are pre-registered (as is required for clinical trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kerr, 1998.

claim: If looking for a sex difference is justified neither by biology nor by prior data, the probability of chancing upon a true positive is lower than for confirmatory research.
source: If looking for a sex difference is justified neither by biology nor by prior data, the probability of chancing upon a true positive is lower than for confirmatory research.
evidence: This is a statistical principle explained by the authors.

claim: When tests are justified by strong prior hypotheses – i.e., in confirmatory studies – subgroup interactions are more likely to be true as they start from a higher pre-test probability.
source: In contrast, when tests are justified by strong prior hypotheses – i.e., in confirmatory studies – subgroup interactions are more likely to be true as they start from a higher pre-test probability.
evidence: This is a statistical principle explained by the authors.

claim: For exploratory studies, even statistically significant findings of sex differences should be treated with caution and caveat.
source: In other words, for exploratory studies, even statistically significant findings of sex differences should be treated with caution and caveat.
evidence: This is a recommendation by the authors.

claim: There is a particular inaccuracy in the reflexive assumption that phenomena observed in females must be driven by estrogens.
source: For example, there is a particular inaccuracy – verging on laziness – in the reflexive assumption that phenomena observed in females must be driven by estrogens.
evidence: This is a critical observation by the authors.

claim: Observational studies must at least consider the role that gendered exposures and experiences might play in sex differences.
source: In terms of alternative explanations, observational studies must at least consider the role that gendered exposures and experiences might play; not every putative sex difference can be explained by the usual "biological" suspects (Ritz and Greaves, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ritz and Greaves, 2022.

claim: Most human societies can be fascinated by sex differences, no matter how small.
source: Finally, we must be wary of sex essentialism and reification. Most human societies (including some study sections and promotions committees) can be fascinated by sex differences, no matter how small.
evidence: This is an observation by the authors about societal attitudes.

claim: The failure to consider large overlap between sexes can lead to inflating the importance of sex differences and reifying notions of sex.
source: The failure to consider large overlap between sexes can lead us to inflate the importance of sex differences and reify notions of sex that our investigations should seek to query.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors.

claim: An over-emphasis on sex, beyond what is warranted by the data, will result in a 'precision medicine' plagued by imprecision – separate treatments for women and men that do not consider individual physiologies or the myriad traits that predict treatment efficacy better than sex.
source: The unfortunate result of an over-emphasis on sex, beyond what is warranted by the data, will be a "precision medicine" plagued by imprecision – separate treatments for women and men that do not consider individual physiologies or the myriad traits that predict treatment efficacy better than sex.
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors about the consequences of over-emphasizing sex differences.

claim: In mandating sex-inclusive research without requiring sound methodology, we are attempting to reap the benefits of exploratory research without the discipline of confirmatory research.
source: In mandating sex-inclusive research without requiring sound methodology, we are attempting to reap the benefits of exploratory research without the discipline of confirmatory research.
evidence: This is a critical observation by the authors about current policies.

claim: In no other arena has one particular subgroup analysis been singled out as appropriate for every study, whether or not the investigators hypothesized differences to begin with.
source: In no other arena has one particular subgroup analysis been singled out as appropriate for every study, whether or not the investigators hypothesized differences to begin with.
evidence: This is an observation by the authors about the uniqueness of sex-based subgroup analysis requirements.

claim: While some of the discoveries of sex differences will prove to be real and meaningful, many will not.
source: While some of these discoveries will prove to be real and in fact meaningful, many will not.
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors based on statistical principles.

claim: The science of sex differences has an interesting future that will almost certainly move us away from sex as a binary category.
source: The science of sex differences has an interesting future that will almost certainly move us away from sex as a binary category.
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors about the future of the field.

claim: As a variable in scientific research, 'sex' is problematic, an imperfect proxy for myriad traits that can covary tightly with each other (but often do not).
source: As a variable in scientific research, "sex" is problematic, an imperfect proxy for myriad traits that can covary tightly with each other (but often do not).
evidence: This is a conceptual statement by the authors.

claim: The difference between exploratory and confirmatory studies will remain, as will the conviction that claims of sex differences should be grounded in solid evidence.
source: Nonetheless, the difference between exploratory and confirmatory studies will remain, as will our conviction that claims of sex differences should be grounded in solid evidence.
evidence: This is a statement of principle by the authors.
